category.name: Phishing & email
category.description: Email, chat and SMS lures against staff: credential harvesting, MFA-bypass kits, malicious attachments, consent phishing and post-click mailbox abuse.

playbooks.name: Credential-harvesting link clicked and password entered
playbooks.summary: Use when a user clicked a link to a fake sign-in page and may have typed their password, before any confirmed misuse of the account.

preparation: Enable URL rewriting and time-of-click detonation on the email gateway for all inbound mail
Confirm proxy or DNS logs record full URLs and the requesting user for at least 90 days
Pre-approve a runbook that lets the SOC force a password reset and revoke sessions without a change ticket
Keep a list of the official sign-in domains for every SaaS app so lookalike pages are quick to spot
identification: Pull the original message from the mailbox and record sender, subject, Message-ID and the harvest URL
Detonate the harvest URL in an isolated sandbox and capture where the form posts credentials
Search proxy logs for every user who requested the harvest domain and note who submitted a POST
Review Entra ID sign-in logs for the clicker for new IPs, countries or user agents after the click time
Interview the user to confirm whether they typed a password or approved an MFA prompt
containment: Reset the password for every user who submitted the form and revoke their refresh tokens
Block the harvest domain and its hosting IP at the secure web gateway and DNS resolver
Purge the message from all mailboxes with a compliance search and purge
Add the sender address and envelope domain to the gateway block list
eradication: Check the affected accounts for new MFA methods, app passwords or registered devices and remove unknown ones
Remove any mailbox forwarding or inbox rules created after the click
Confirm the same password was not reused on VPN, payroll or other non-SSO systems and reset there too
recovery: Have each affected user re-register MFA in person or over a verified video call
Watch the affected accounts for sign-ins from new locations for 14 days
Submit the harvest URL to the hosting provider and browser safe-browsing services for takedown
lessons: Measure time from first click to password reset and set a target for the next event
Decide whether phishing-resistant MFA should be required for the users who were targeted
Add a detection for POST requests to newly registered domains from browsers on corporate devices
Feed the lure text and sender into the next phishing awareness exercise

splunk.title: Users who reached the harvest domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_method) as methods min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by Web.user Web.src | convert ctime(first_seen)

splunk.title: Sign-ins for clickers after the lure arrived
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName IN (<suspect_user>) earliest=-7d | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips values(location.countryOrRegion) as countries values(appDisplayName) as apps by userPrincipalName status.errorCode

splunk.title: Recipients of the phishing message
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<sender>" OR All_Email.subject="<subject>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.action

playbooks.name: Adversary-in-the-middle phish stole session cookie and bypassed MFA
playbooks.summary: Use when an EvilProxy- or Evilginx-style reverse proxy captured a user's session token, so MFA was satisfied and the attacker signed in with a stolen cookie.

preparation: Enable Entra ID risk detections for anomalous token and token issuer anomaly alerts
Require compliant or hybrid-joined devices for access to Exchange Online and SharePoint
Roll out FIDO2 or Windows Hello for Business to staff with access to finance and admin roles
Retain Entra sign-in and non-interactive sign-in logs in the SIEM for at least 180 days
identification: Find the sign-in where MFA succeeded from the proxy IP and note the session ID and correlation ID
Compare the user agent and IP of the original sign-in with later non-interactive sign-ins using the same session
Identify the reverse-proxy hostname from proxy logs and check whether it mirrors the Microsoft login page
List every mailbox, Graph and SharePoint action taken from the attacker IP after token theft
Check whether the attacker registered a new authenticator app or phone number on the account
containment: Revoke all refresh tokens and sessions for the user with Revoke-MgUserSignInSession
Block the attacker IPs and the proxy domain with a Conditional Access named location and web filter
Disable the account temporarily if attacker activity continues after token revocation
Search all sign-in logs for other users authenticating through the same proxy IP range
eradication: Delete attacker-added MFA methods and require re-registration with a phishing-resistant method
Remove OAuth grants, inbox rules and mail forwarding created during the attacker session
Reset the password even though it was not the main access path, since the proxy also captured it
recovery: Enable token protection or sign-in session binding for the affected user group where licensed
Confirm the user's mailbox contents and sent items show no further attacker messages
Notify recipients of any internal phish the attacker sent from the account during the session
lessons: Record why Conditional Access did not stop a sign-in from an unmanaged device
Add a detection for successful MFA from an IP that has never been seen for that user and is hosting-provider ASN
Track the share of privileged users still on push or SMS MFA and set a deadline to move them

splunk.title: Same session used from more than one IP
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName=<suspect_user> earliest=-3d | stats dc(ipAddress) as ip_count values(ipAddress) as ips values(userAgent) as agents by sessionId | where ip_count>1

splunk.title: Other users signing in from the proxy IPs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin ipAddress IN (<ioc_ip>) | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(appDisplayName) as apps by userPrincipalName | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Mailbox actions from the attacker IP
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity ClientIP=<ioc_ip> | stats count values(Operation) as ops by UserId Workload

playbooks.name: QR-code phishing email led users to a fake login on their phones
playbooks.summary: Use when a message carried a QR code (often in a PDF or image) that sent users to a credential page on a personal or unmanaged mobile device, outside corporate web filtering.

preparation: Enable QR-code decoding and URL extraction in the email gateway image and PDF scanners
Enroll corporate phones in MDM with a mobile threat defense app that filters malicious URLs
Block sign-in to corporate apps from unmanaged mobile browsers with Conditional Access app protection
identification: Decode the QR code from the attachment image in a sandbox and record the destination URL
Search mail logs for messages with the same attachment hash or image dimensions sent to other staff
Review Entra sign-ins with mobile user agents for recipients in the hours after delivery
Ask recipients whether they scanned the code and on which device, corporate or personal
containment: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for users who scanned the code and entered credentials
Purge the QR message from mailboxes using the attachment hash as the search key
Block the decoded domain in DNS filtering and in the MDM web filter profile
eradication: Remove attacker-registered MFA devices from the accounts that signed in from unknown mobile IPs
Check the scanned-from phones for a malicious configuration profile or rogue VPN profile
Add the PDF sender pattern and QR image hash to the gateway block list
recovery: Re-enable affected users after they confirm MFA methods and device list in a verified call
Send staff a short notice showing the lure and explaining that QR codes in email are treated as links
Confirm the decoded phishing domain has been reported to the registrar and taken down
lessons: Record whether the gateway decoded the QR code, and if not, raise the gap with the vendor
Add a detection for sign-ins from personal mobile devices immediately after a QR-bearing message
Decide whether to quarantine all inbound mail where the only content is an image with a QR code

splunk.title: Messages carrying the QR attachment
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.file_hash="<attachment_hash>" OR All_Email.file_name="<attachment_name>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.src_user All_Email.action

splunk.title: Mobile sign-ins by recipients after delivery
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName IN (<recipient_list>) earliest=-48h | search deviceDetail.operatingSystem IN (iOS, Android) | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips values(deviceDetail.isCompliant) as compliant by userPrincipalName status.errorCode

playbooks.name: OAuth consent phishing granted a malicious app mailbox access
playbooks.summary: Use when a user clicked a consent prompt that granted a third-party app permissions such as Mail.Read or offline_access, giving persistent access that a password reset does not remove.

preparation: Restrict user consent to verified publishers and low-risk permissions in Entra enterprise app settings
Turn on the admin consent workflow so users can request apps instead of granting them
Ingest Entra audit logs with Consent to application events into the SIEM
identification: Find the Consent to application audit event and record the app ID, publisher and granted scopes
Check whether the app is multi-tenant, unverified and was created recently in its home tenant
List every user in the tenant who consented to the same app ID
Review Microsoft Graph activity logs for API calls made by the app's service principal
containment: Disable the malicious service principal so it can no longer obtain tokens
Revoke the delegated permission grants for the app with Remove-MgOauth2PermissionGrant
Block the app ID tenant-wide by setting it as not allowed for user sign-in
eradication: Delete the service principal after evidence has been exported
Check consenting users for inbox rules or sent mail created through Graph by the app
Remove any certificate or secret the attacker added to other app registrations in the tenant
recovery: Tell affected users what data the app could read and what was actually accessed
Re-run an inventory of all third-party apps with high-privilege scopes and review owners
Re-enable user consent only for verified publishers once the app review is complete
lessons: Track how many apps still hold Mail.ReadWrite or Files.ReadWrite.All grants from user consent
Add a detection for consent to an unverified app requesting offline_access plus mail scopes
Decide whether to block user consent entirely for the departments that were targeted

splunk.title: Consent grants to the suspect app
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation="Consent to application." | search ModifiedProperties{}.NewValue="*<app_id>*" OR Target{}.ID="*<app_id>*" | stats count min(_time) as first by UserId ClientIP | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: All recent consents to unverified apps
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=AzureActiveDirectory Operation="Consent to application." earliest=-30d | stats count dc(UserId) as users values(UserId) as consenting_users by ObjectId | sort - users

splunk.title: Mail access by the app after consent
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange Operation=MailItemsAccessed AppId=<app_id> | stats count sum(OperationCount) as items by MailboxOwnerUPN ClientIPAddress

playbooks.name: Malicious attachment opened and dropped a loader
playbooks.summary: Use when a user opened an emailed document, ISO, LNK or archive that launched a script or loader on their workstation, and endpoint compromise is suspected.

preparation: Block inbound ISO, IMG, VHD, LNK, HTA and JS attachments at the mail gateway
Enable ASR rules that stop Office apps from creating child processes and executable content
Make sure EDR can isolate a host and pull a triage package remotely
identification: Retrieve the attachment from quarantine or the mailbox and hash it in a sandbox
Trace the process tree from the opening app on the host in EDR and note spawned interpreters
Record files written to user temp and AppData and any scheduled tasks or Run keys created
List outbound connections from the host in the hour after the attachment was opened
Search mail logs for the same attachment hash delivered to other mailboxes
containment: Isolate the workstation in EDR while keeping it powered on for memory capture
Block the C2 domains and IPs seen from the host at the firewall and proxy
Purge the attachment from every mailbox and add its hash to the EDR block list
Disable the user's account sessions if the loader ran in their logged-on context
eradication: Remove the dropped payload, persistence entries and any added local accounts
Reimage the workstation if a second-stage payload or credential dumping was observed
Reset passwords for the user and any account that logged on to the host since infection
recovery: Return the rebuilt host to the user after a clean EDR scan and patch check
Hunt across the fleet for the loader's file path and mutex for 30 days
Restore the user's documents from OneDrive version history if the payload altered files
lessons: Record which file type got through and whether the gateway should block it
Check whether Mark-of-the-Web was bypassed by the container format and tune ASR accordingly
Measure time from open to isolation and the dwell time before the first alert

splunk.title: Processes spawned by Office or archive tools
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest=<host> Processes.parent_process_name IN (winword.exe, excel.exe, outlook.exe, explorer.exe) Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe, mshta.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe) by Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Other recipients of the attachment
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.file_hash="<attachment_hash>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.action All_Email.src_user

splunk.title: Network connections from the infected host
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=3 host=<host> earliest=-24h | stats count values(DestinationPort) as ports by Image DestinationIp DestinationHostname

playbooks.name: Callback phishing: user phoned a fake support number and installed remote tool
playbooks.summary: Use when a telephone-oriented attack delivery email (fake invoice or subscription renewal) got a user to call a number, after which a caller talked them into installing remote access software.

preparation: Maintain an allow list of approved remote support tools and block others with application control
Give the help desk a script for staff who report a call that asked them to install software
Log process creation on workstations so remote tool installs show up in the SIEM
identification: Collect the lure email and record the phone number, fake invoice amount and brand impersonated
Ask the user for the call time, what the caller asked them to do and any codes they read out
Find remote access tool installs on the host in EDR, such as AnyDesk, ScreenConnect or Quick Assist sessions
Review the remote session duration and files transferred during it from the tool's own logs
Search mail logs for the same phone number or invoice text sent to other users
containment: Isolate the workstation and end any live remote session
Block the remote tool's relay domains at the proxy for unapproved instances
Freeze any online banking or payroll session the user had open during the call
eradication: Uninstall the remote tool and remove any service or startup entry it created
Check for credential stores accessed, new browser extensions or downloaded payloads during the session
Reset passwords the user typed while the caller watched the screen
recovery: Reimage the host if the caller ran scripts or downloaded binaries during the session
Have the user confirm with their bank or card issuer that no payment was made to the caller
Restore normal network access after a full EDR scan returns clean
lessons: Add an alert for first-seen remote access tool execution on any workstation
Note that the email had no link or attachment and check why the gateway let it through
Include callback lures with phone numbers in the next awareness campaign

splunk.title: Remote access tools started on the host
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest=<host> Processes.process_name IN (anydesk.exe, screenconnect*.exe, quickassist.exe, teamviewer.exe, rustdesk.exe, splashtop*.exe) by Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Fleet-wide first-seen remote tools
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as first dc(Processes.dest) as hosts from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (anydesk.exe, screenconnect*.exe, rustdesk.exe, atera*.exe) by Processes.process_name | where first>relative_time(now(), "-7d") | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Lure emails with the callback number
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace Subject IN ("*invoice*", "*renewal*", "*subscription*") earliest=-7d | stats count values(RecipientAddress) as recipients by SenderAddress Subject

playbooks.name: Targeted spear-phish against an executive
playbooks.summary: Use when a tailored lure aimed at a named executive or their assistant references real projects, board events or travel, and the target may have clicked or replied.

preparation: Maintain a VIP list in the email gateway so messages to executives get stricter impersonation checks
Agree in advance which executive assistant and chief of staff to contact for VIP incidents
Enable mailbox auditing at the E5 level for executives, including MailItemsAccessed
identification: Record which public details the lure used, such as board meeting dates or a recent press release
Check whether the executive, their delegate or their assistant clicked, replied or forwarded the lure
Review mailbox delegate access and Send As permissions on the executive mailbox
Search for the same sender infrastructure targeting other members of the leadership team
Review the executive's sign-ins and device registrations for the past 30 days
containment: Reset credentials and revoke sessions for the executive and any delegate who interacted with the lure
Block the sender domain and add display-name impersonation rules for the executive's name
Brief the executive and assistant in person about the attempt and any follow-up to expect
eradication: Remove unknown delegates, forwarding rules or mobile devices from the executive mailbox
Confirm no calendar items or contact records were planted to support a later pretext
Remove the lure and any follow-up messages from all leadership mailboxes
recovery: Move the executive and their assistant to phishing-resistant MFA if not already in place
Keep enhanced monitoring on the VIP mailboxes for 30 days
Prepare a short brief for the leadership team describing the lure and what to watch for
lessons: Review how much executive information is public on the company website and social profiles
Measure whether VIP impersonation rules fired and tune them for the lure style seen
Decide whether executive assistants need their own targeted training

splunk.title: Mail to the leadership list from the attacker domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="*@<ioc_domain>" All_Email.recipient IN (<vip_list>) by All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.action

splunk.title: Delegate and permission changes on VIP mailboxes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange Operation IN (Add-MailboxPermission, Add-RecipientPermission, Set-Mailbox, New-InboxRule, Add-MailboxFolderPermission) ObjectId IN (<vip_mailbox>) earliest=-30d | table _time UserId Operation ObjectId Parameters{}.Value

playbooks.name: Reply-chain thread hijack delivered malware in an existing conversation
playbooks.summary: Use when attackers replied inside a genuine email thread, stolen from another organization's compromised mailbox, with a link or attachment that recipients trusted because the conversation was real.

preparation: Keep a contact path for security teams at key partners and suppliers
Tag inbound mail from external senders with a visible banner even inside existing threads
Enable gateway detection for In-Reply-To headers that do not match previous sender infrastructure
identification: Compare the headers of the hijacked reply with earlier genuine messages in the thread
Identify whose mailbox the thread was stolen from by checking which side's messages were quoted
Find every internal recipient of the hijacked reply and whether they opened the link or file
Analyze the payload in a sandbox and pull C2 indicators
Check whether the reply came from the partner's real server or a lookalike domain
containment: Purge the hijacked reply from all mailboxes by Message-ID
Block the payload hosting URL and C2 indicators at proxy and DNS
Isolate any host where the attachment was executed
eradication: Notify the partner's security team that their mailbox appears compromised and share headers
Remove payload artifacts from affected hosts and reset credentials used on them
Temporarily quarantine further mail from the partner domain until they confirm cleanup
recovery: Release held partner mail after the partner confirms the compromised account is secured
Tell staff who are in the thread to verify any new request from that partner by phone
Lift isolation on hosts after EDR confirms no persistence
lessons: Record how long the partner mailbox was compromised before anyone noticed
Add a detection for replies whose sending IP differs from earlier messages in the same thread
Review whether partner domains should be exempt from attachment sandboxing

splunk.title: Recipients of the hijacked reply
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace MessageId="<message_id>" OR (SenderAddress="<sender>" Subject="RE:*<thread_subject>*") | stats count values(Status) as status by RecipientAddress FromIP

splunk.title: Clicks on the payload URL
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by Web.user Web.src Web.http_user_agent | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: Compromised internal mailbox sending phish to coworkers
playbooks.summary: Use when one of your own accounts was taken over and is sending phishing mail to colleagues, so the messages pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC and look fully internal.

preparation: Set outbound spam policies with low recipient-rate limits for normal users
Create a mail-flow alert for an internal user sending to more than 50 internal recipients in an hour
Make sure the SOC can block a user from sending mail without disabling the account
identification: List every message the compromised account sent since the first suspicious sign-in
Identify the attacker sign-in that preceded the send burst and record IP and user agent
Check the sent items for deleted messages using the Recoverable Items folder
Find coworkers who clicked links in the internal phish using proxy logs
Review the account's inbox rules for ones that hide replies from recipients
containment: Block outbound mail from the account and revoke all its sessions
Reset the account password and remove attacker MFA methods
Purge the internal phish from every recipient mailbox
Treat every coworker who entered credentials as a new compromised account
eradication: Delete inbox rules that moved replies to RSS Feeds, Archive or Deleted Items
Remove any OAuth apps or mailbox delegates added by the attacker
Check whether the attacker downloaded the global address list for later campaigns
recovery: Lift the outbound mail block once the account is clean and MFA re-registered
Send an all-staff note from a known account telling people to ignore the earlier messages
Contact any external recipients who also received the phish from the account
lessons: Measure how many internal recipients clicked before the first report
Check whether the outbound spam policy restricted the account and at what volume
Add a detection for a single internal sender with many messages carrying the same external link

splunk.title: Messages sent by the compromised account
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Email.recipient) as recipients from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<suspect_user>" by All_Email.subject _time span=1h

splunk.title: Internal senders with unusual recipient counts
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace SenderAddress="*@<your_domain>" earliest=-24h | bin _time span=1h | stats dc(RecipientAddress) as rcpts by SenderAddress _time | where rcpts>50

splunk.title: Inbox rules created on the account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation IN (New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule, UpdateInboxRules) UserId=<suspect_user> | table _time ClientIP Operation Parameters{}.Name Parameters{}.Value

playbooks.name: SharePoint or OneDrive file-share lure led to credential theft
playbooks.summary: Use when users received a genuine-looking 'shared a file with you' notification, often from a compromised tenant, that pointed to a document containing a link to a credential page.

preparation: Restrict external sharing so files from untrusted tenants open with a warning
Make sure proxy logs capture the full sharepoint.com path, not only the hostname
Configure Safe Links to scan links inside Office documents opened from SharePoint
identification: Identify the sharing tenant and the account that sent the share notification
Open the shared document in a sandbox and extract the embedded link
Find users who opened the shared file URL and those who then reached the credential page
Check whether the share came from a partner tenant you already trust
containment: Reset credentials for users who reached the credential page and submitted a form
Block the specific SharePoint path at the proxy without blocking the whole tenant domain
Purge the share notification emails and report the file to Microsoft as phishing
eradication: Remove any guest accounts the attacker tenant created in your directory
Delete files the compromised users may have shared outward after the click
Notify the sharing organization that their account is sending lures
recovery: Confirm affected users can access their own OneDrive and files are unchanged
Review the external sharing allow list with the collaboration team
Monitor for the same tenant sending new share invites for two weeks
lessons: Track how often trusted cloud storage domains are used to host lures in your mail flow
Add a detection for proxy hits to an external tenant's SharePoint followed by a non-Microsoft login page
Decide whether to require guest access approval for new external tenants

splunk.title: Users who opened the shared document
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<attacker_tenant>.sharepoint.com*" by Web.user Web.url | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Share notifications received
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace SenderAddress="no-reply@sharepointonline.com" Subject="*shared*" earliest=-3d | stats count values(RecipientAddress) as recipients by Subject

playbooks.name: Fake DocuSign or e-signature request phish
playbooks.summary: Use when staff received a counterfeit e-signature envelope, or a real envelope from a malicious account, whose Review Document button led to a credential page or malware download.

preparation: Record which e-signature vendors the company actually uses and the sending addresses they use
Ask legal and procurement to tell the SOC when they expect envelopes from a new counterparty
Enable gateway rules that flag e-signature brand names in mail not from the vendor's sending domains
identification: Check whether the envelope came from the vendor's real sending infrastructure or a spoofed domain
If real, record the sender account inside the e-signature platform and the envelope ID
Follow the Review Document link in a sandbox and record the final landing domain
Ask legal or finance whether any real agreement with that counterparty was expected
containment: Purge the envelope email from all inboxes
Block the final landing domain and any redirect domains in the chain
Reset credentials for users who submitted a password on the landing page
eradication: Report the abusive sender account and envelope ID to the e-signature vendor's abuse team
Check affected accounts for new MFA devices or mail rules
Add the lookalike sending domain to the block list
recovery: Remind finance and legal of the approved way to confirm unexpected signature requests
Release any genuine envelopes that were caught in the purge
Track whether the vendor disabled the abusive account
lessons: Measure how many users clicked versus reported this lure compared with generic phish
Add a detection for e-signature-themed subjects from senders outside the vendor's domains
Consider publishing an internal page listing the e-signature vendors in use

splunk.title: E-signature themed mail from non-vendor senders
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*DocuSign*", "*sign*document*", "*envelope*") NOT All_Email.src_user IN ("*@docusign.net", "*@docusign.com") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject All_Email.recipient

splunk.title: Visits to the landing domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by Web.user Web.src

playbooks.name: Fake voicemail notification phish with audio attachment or link
playbooks.summary: Use when users received a missed-call or voicemail notification, often with an HTML or audio file, that led to a sign-in page dressed up as the phone system or Microsoft 365.

preparation: Document what genuine voicemail notifications from the company phone platform look like
Block or sandbox HTML and HTM attachments from external senders
Make sure the gateway logs attachment names and file types
identification: Open the HTML attachment in a sandbox and decode any base64 or JavaScript that builds the page
Record where the embedded form sends credentials and any pre-filled email address in the page
List recipients who opened the attachment using endpoint file-open telemetry or browser history
Check whether the message spoofs the internal phone system's sender name
containment: Purge all voicemail-themed messages with the same attachment hash or naming pattern
Block the credential POST endpoint domain at the proxy
Reset passwords for any user whose browser posted to that endpoint
eradication: Add a transport rule that quarantines external mail using the phone system's display name
Remove attacker MFA registrations from affected accounts
Report the credential endpoint to its hosting provider
recovery: Tell staff how real voicemails are delivered so they can spot future fakes
Release legitimate voicemail notifications from quarantine if the rule caught any
Watch affected accounts for new sign-ins for 14 days
lessons: Count how many voicemail lures arrived in the past quarter and whether HTML blocking would have stopped them
Add a detection for browsers posting form data to domains first seen in the last 7 days
Review whether the phone platform can stop emailing voicemails as attachments

splunk.title: Voicemail-themed messages with HTML attachments
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*voicemail*", "*missed call*", "*voice message*") All_Email.file_name IN ("*.htm", "*.html", "*.shtml") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.file_name

splunk.title: Credential POSTs to the phish endpoint
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by Web.user Web.src Web.url

playbooks.name: Malicious calendar invites injected into staff calendars
playbooks.summary: Use when external meeting invites with phishing links appear on users' calendars automatically, bypassing inbox filtering because the calendar app added them on receipt.

preparation: Set calendar policy so invites from unknown external senders are not added automatically
Know which admin tool can remove events from all calendars in bulk for your platform
Include calendar items in compliance search scope
identification: Record the organizer address, event title and link in the invite body
Search all calendars for events from the same organizer or with the same link
Check proxy logs for users who opened the link from the calendar reminder
Confirm whether the invite arrived via email or through a shared calendar subscription
containment: Delete the malicious events from every calendar with a bulk removal or purge
Block the link domain at the proxy
Block the organizer domain from sending calendar invites
eradication: Reset credentials for any user who submitted details on the linked page
Remove unwanted calendar subscriptions added by the invite
Report the organizer account to its mail provider
recovery: Tell staff that invites from unknown senders may now need to be accepted manually
Check that legitimate external meeting invites still arrive after the policy change
Confirm no deleted event belonged to a real external meeting
lessons: Track whether calendar invites are now a regular lure channel in your environment
Add a detection for external organizers sending invites to many users at once
Decide if calendar auto-add from external domains should stay disabled

splunk.title: Invites from the organizer to many users
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace SenderAddress="<sender>" earliest=-7d | stats dc(RecipientAddress) as recipients values(Subject) as subjects by SenderAddress

splunk.title: Google Workspace calendar events from external organizer
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=gws:reports:calendar event.name=create_event organizer_calendar_id="*@<ioc_domain>" | stats count values(target_calendar_id) as calendars by event_title

playbooks.name: Mass phishing campaign hit hundreds of mailboxes at once
playbooks.summary: Use when a high-volume campaign landed in many mailboxes within minutes and the priority is fast scoping, bulk purge and finding the few users who clicked.

preparation: Keep a tested compliance search and purge procedure that can run against all mailboxes
Pre-build a SIEM dashboard of recipients, clickers and reporters keyed by Message-ID or subject
Agree with communications on a template banner or all-staff alert for active campaigns
identification: Cluster the campaign by sender IPs, subjects, URLs and attachment hashes to catch all variants
Count delivered versus quarantined messages and list the delivered recipients
Pull click logs from the gateway's URL rewriting service for the campaign URLs
Separate clickers from credential submitters using proxy POST data
Note how many users reported the message and how quickly
containment: Run a bulk purge across all variants rather than one subject line at a time
Block every campaign URL domain and sending IP at the gateway
Force password resets for the credential submitters
eradication: Add the campaign's sending infrastructure to gateway block rules for 30 days
Check submitters' accounts for rules, MFA devices and app consent changes
Re-run the cluster search an hour later to catch late-arriving variants
recovery: Post a brief all-staff alert showing the lure and confirming it has been removed
Thank reporters and close out their tickets with the outcome
Release false-positive quarantined mail caught by the broad purge
lessons: Record delivered count, click rate, submit rate and time to purge for trend tracking
Identify which variant evaded the gateway and send samples to the vendor
Check whether the report-phish button volume helped scoping and how to speed that up

splunk.title: Campaign variants by sender and subject
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Email.recipient) as recipients from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_ip IN (<ioc_ip>) OR All_Email.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject All_Email.action | sort - recipients

splunk.title: Clicks on campaign URLs from the gateway
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:defender:atp:alerts OR sourcetype=ms:o365:safelinks Url="*<ioc_domain>*" | stats count values(Action) as action by UserId Url

splunk.title: Credential submissions to campaign domains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url IN ("*<ioc_domain>*") by Web.user Web.src

playbooks.name: Single user-reported suspicious email needs triage
playbooks.summary: Use for the routine case of one user reporting one suspicious message: decide quickly if it is malicious, spam or legitimate, and scope it before closing.

preparation: Deploy a report-phish button that forwards the original message with full headers
Keep a triage checklist covering headers, links, attachments and sender reputation
Set an SLA for responding to user phishing reports
identification: Parse the reported message headers and check SPF, DKIM and DMARC results
Check each URL and attachment hash against threat intel and the gateway verdict
Search mail logs for other recipients of the same message
Ask the reporter whether they clicked, opened or replied before reporting
Classify the message as malicious, spam, simulation or legitimate
containment: Purge the message from other recipients if it is classified as malicious
Block the sender or URL if it is not already blocked
Escalate to the credential-harvest or attachment playbook if anyone interacted
eradication: Add confirmed indicators to the gateway and proxy block lists
Submit the sample to the email security vendor as a false negative
Remove the sender from any user safe-sender lists
recovery: Reply to the reporter with the verdict and thank them
Release the message back to the reporter if it was legitimate
Close the ticket with the classification and indicators recorded
lessons: Track report-to-verdict time and the share of reports that were real phish
Find senders that are reported often but are legitimate and fix their authentication
Use common reported lures as examples in awareness training

splunk.title: Other recipients of the reported message
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.message_id="<message_id>" OR (All_Email.src_user="<sender>" All_Email.subject="<subject>") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.action

splunk.title: Did anyone visit the reported URL
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by Web.user Web.http_method

playbooks.name: Phish bypassed the secure email gateway and reached inboxes
playbooks.summary: Use when a malicious message was delivered despite the gateway, and you need to know why: allow-list abuse, direct-to-tenant delivery, time-delayed weaponization or a scanner blind spot.

preparation: Lock down the tenant so inbound mail is only accepted from the gateway's IP ranges
Keep an inventory of gateway allow-list entries with an owner and expiry date
Make sure gateway verdict logs and tenant message trace both flow into the SIEM
identification: Trace the message path in the headers and confirm whether it passed through the gateway at all
Check whether the sender, domain or IP matched an allow-list or bypass rule
Compare the gateway verdict at delivery time with a rescan of the URL or file now
Check whether the URL was benign at delivery and weaponized later
Search for other messages delivered by the same bypass path in the last 30 days
containment: Remove the allow-list entry or bypass rule that let the message in
Block direct-to-tenant SMTP from non-gateway IPs with a connector restriction
Purge the delivered message and any similar ones found through the same path
eradication: Submit the sample to the gateway vendor as a missed detection with full headers
Enable time-of-click URL rescanning if delivery-time scanning was the only control
Escalate any clicks to the matching phishing playbook
recovery: Confirm legitimate mail from the removed allow-list sender still arrives through normal scanning
Re-test the connector restriction by sending a message directly to the tenant MX
Inform the vendor relationship owner about the bypass and requested fix
lessons: Review all remaining allow-list entries and remove those without a current business owner
Add a detection for inbound messages lacking the gateway's stamp header
Track gateway miss rate per quarter using user reports as the ground truth

splunk.title: Inbound mail not received from gateway IPs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace Direction=Inbound earliest=-7d NOT FromIP IN (<gateway_ip_ranges>) | stats count values(SenderAddress) as senders by FromIP | sort - count

splunk.title: Messages delivered by allow-list rule
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<gateway_sourcetype> action=delivered policy=*allow* earliest=-30d | stats count values(recipient) as recipients by sender policy

playbooks.name: Lookalike of the company domain registered
playbooks.summary: Use when brand monitoring or a user report shows a newly registered domain that imitates your company domain, before or just after it is used in phishing or fraud.

preparation: Subscribe to a domain monitoring feed that alerts on typo and homoglyph variants of company domains
Keep evidence templates and contacts for registrar abuse teams and the legal team
Know which defensive domain registrations the company already owns
identification: Record registrar, registration date, name servers and MX records for the lookalike
Check whether the domain has MX records or an SPF record that suggest it will send mail
Screenshot any website on the domain and check if it clones your login or careers page
Search mail logs for inbound or outbound mail involving the lookalike
Search proxy logs for staff visiting the domain
containment: Block the lookalike domain in the email gateway, proxy and DNS resolver
Add the lookalike to a transport rule that quarantines mail from it
Warn finance and HR that mail from the lookalike is fraudulent
eradication: File an abuse report with the registrar and hosting provider including trademark evidence
Ask legal whether a UDRP complaint is warranted if the registrar declines
Request takedown through browser safe-browsing reporting if a phishing page is live
recovery: Confirm the domain is suspended or the site is offline and keep it on the block list
Register remaining high-risk variants defensively
Tell customers or partners if mail from the lookalike reached them
lessons: Measure time from registration to detection and to takedown
Add the lookalike pattern to the gateway's impersonation detection
Review whether domain monitoring covers all brand names and subsidiaries

splunk.title: Mail involving the lookalike domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="*@<lookalike_domain>" OR All_Email.recipient="*@<lookalike_domain>" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject

splunk.title: DNS lookups of the lookalike
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns query="*<lookalike_domain>" | stats count min(_time) as first by src query | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: Phishing impersonating the company is targeting customers
playbooks.summary: Use when customers report emails or sites pretending to be your company, asking them to log in, pay or download something, and the company must protect customers and its brand.

preparation: Publish DMARC at p=reject for all company domains, including ones that do not send mail
Set up a customer-facing address for reporting suspicious messages that claim to be from the company
Agree with communications and support on a holding statement for customer impersonation
identification: Collect samples from customer reports with full headers and the phishing URL
Check DMARC aggregate reports for spoofed mail claiming to be from your domain
Identify the phishing site host, registrar and whether it clones the customer portal
Check customer portal logs for logins from the attacker IPs after the campaign started
containment: Submit takedown requests to the host and registrar for the phishing site
Report the site to browser safe-browsing services and anti-phishing working groups
Force password resets for customer accounts seen logging in from attacker IPs
Post a notice on the support site describing the scam and how to verify real messages
eradication: Move DMARC to reject if it was still at none or quarantine
Add attacker IPs to the customer portal's sign-in risk rules
Track takedown tickets until each site is offline
recovery: Brief the customer support team on how to handle affected customers
Monitor for the campaign returning on new domains for 30 days
Contact customers who reported losses and route them to the fraud team
lessons: Record time to takedown for each phishing site and the slowest providers
Add customer portal detections for credential stuffing from campaign infrastructure
Decide whether to adopt BIMI or a brand monitoring service

splunk.title: Customer portal logins from campaign IPs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Authentication.user) as users from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=<customer_portal> Authentication.src IN (<ioc_ip>) by Authentication.src Authentication.action

splunk.title: Portal traffic referred from the phishing site
splunk.spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined referer="*<ioc_domain>*" | stats count values(uri_path) as paths by clientip

playbooks.name: SMS smishing campaign targeting staff phones
playbooks.summary: Use when employees receive text messages pretending to be IT, HR or a delivery service with links to fake login or MFA pages, outside any email control.

preparation: Tell staff that IT never sends login links by SMS and publish how to report smishing
Enable mobile threat defense URL filtering on managed phones
Know which staff phone numbers are listed publicly or in data broker sites
identification: Collect screenshots of the texts with sender number, time and URL
Check the URL in a sandbox and identify the brand cloned on the page
Search Entra or Okta sign-ins for affected users from new devices after the texts arrived
Estimate how attackers got the phone numbers, such as a vendor leak or public directory
Count how many staff received the text using reports and help desk tickets
containment: Block the smishing domain in DNS filtering and the mobile threat defense policy
Reset passwords and revoke sessions for any staff who entered credentials
Send an urgent notice to all staff with a picture of the text
eradication: Report the sender number to the carrier's spam reporting short code
Remove attacker-added MFA devices from affected accounts
Ask the domain registrar to suspend the smishing domain
recovery: Confirm affected users can sign in normally with their own devices
Watch for follow-up voice calls to the same staff group
Close help desk tickets with guidance on spotting future texts
lessons: Track whether the source of leaked phone numbers was identified
Add a detection for sign-ins with device names or user agents first seen after a smishing wave
Decide whether frontline or shift staff need different reporting channels

splunk.title: Okta sign-ins by targeted staff from new devices
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 eventType IN (user.session.start, user.authentication.auth_via_mfa) actor.alternateId IN (<recipient_list>) earliest=-48h | stats count values(client.ipAddress) as ips values(client.userAgent.rawUserAgent) as agents by actor.alternateId outcome.result

splunk.title: DNS lookups of the smishing domain
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns query="*<ioc_domain>*" | stats count by src query

playbooks.name: Phishing through external Teams or Slack chat messages
playbooks.summary: Use when an outside account messaged staff through Microsoft Teams external access or Slack Connect, posing as IT support or a partner, with a link or file.

preparation: Restrict Teams external access to an allow list of partner domains
Require approval before new Slack Connect channels or DMs with outside organizations
Make sure Teams and Slack audit logs reach the SIEM
identification: Record the external tenant or workspace, display name and message content
Find every user who received a chat request from the same external account
Check whether recipients accepted the chat, clicked the link or downloaded the file
Review endpoints of those who accepted for remote tool installs or downloads
containment: Block the external tenant domain in Teams admin or disconnect the Slack Connect org
Delete the messages and files shared through the chat where the platform allows
Isolate any endpoint where a downloaded file was run
eradication: Reset credentials of users who entered them on a linked page
Remove any remote support tool installed at the attacker's request
Report the external tenant to Microsoft or Slack trust and safety
recovery: Tell staff that IT will never contact them by external chat
Review the external access allow list with business owners
Watch for new external chat requests from similar display names
lessons: Track whether external chat phishing is replacing email phishing in your logs
Add a detection for external one-to-one chats with users outside known partner domains
Decide whether to block external access for users who do not need it

splunk.title: Teams chats created with external users
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation IN (ChatCreated, MessageSent) CommunicationType=OneOnOne | search ParticipantInfo.HasForeignTenantUsers=true | stats count values(UserId) as users by ChatThreadId

splunk.title: Slack Connect invites from unknown organizations
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=slack:audit action IN (connect_dm_invite_sent, shared_channel_invite_accepted) earliest=-7d | stats count values(actor.user.email) as actors by context.location.domain

playbooks.name: Malicious inbox rules created after a phishing click
playbooks.summary: Use when a mailbox has new rules that forward, delete or hide mail (often matching words like invoice or payment) after a user fell for a phish, signalling hands-on mailbox abuse.

preparation: Block automatic external forwarding in the outbound spam policy
Alert on new inbox rules that move mail to RSS Feeds, Conversation History or Deleted Items
Keep a script that exports all inbox rules for a mailbox with creation time
identification: Export every inbox rule on the mailbox with Get-InboxRule and note conditions and actions
Find the New-InboxRule audit event and the client IP that created each rule
Identify keywords in the rule conditions, such as wire, payment or the CFO's name
Check whether forwarded mail left the tenant and to which external addresses
Look for the same rule names or patterns on other mailboxes in the tenant
containment: Disable and export the malicious rules before deleting them
Revoke sessions and reset the password for the mailbox owner
Block the forwarding destination address at the gateway
eradication: Delete the malicious rules and any SMTP forwarding set on the mailbox
Restore mail the rules moved or deleted from Recoverable Items
Remove any OWA or mobile device sessions the attacker used
recovery: Review the restored hidden mail with the user for fraud attempts the attacker intercepted
Warn contacts in the hidden threads if the attacker replied to them
Keep a rule-creation alert on the mailbox for 30 days
lessons: Record how long the rules existed before discovery
Add a detection for rules with financial keywords that also delete or move mail
Confirm external auto-forwarding is blocked for all users, not just the affected one

splunk.title: Inbox rule creation with hide or forward actions
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation IN (New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule) earliest=-30d | search Parameters{}.Name IN (MoveToFolder, DeleteMessage, ForwardTo, RedirectTo, ForwardAsAttachmentTo) | table _time UserId ClientIP Parameters{}.Name Parameters{}.Value

splunk.title: Mailbox forwarding set via Set-Mailbox
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation=Set-Mailbox Parameters{}.Name IN (ForwardingSmtpAddress, ForwardingAddress, DeliverToMailboxAndForward) | table _time UserId ObjectId ClientIP Parameters{}.Value

playbooks.name: Spoofed mail from the company's own domain failing DMARC
playbooks.summary: Use when messages that claim to come from your own domain or a key partner's domain fail SPF or DKIM alignment yet still reach inboxes, signalling DMARC policy or enforcement gaps.

preparation: Collect DMARC aggregate and forensic reports in a parser that the SOC can query
Inventory every legitimate service that sends mail as the company domain
Configure the gateway to honour sender DMARC p=reject and p=quarantine
identification: Read the Authentication-Results header of the spoofed message and record SPF, DKIM and DMARC verdicts
Check the published DMARC record for the spoofed domain and its policy
Find the sending IPs in DMARC aggregate reports and whether they belong to any known service
List recipients and whether the gateway delivered, quarantined or rejected each message
containment: Purge delivered spoofed messages from mailboxes
Add a transport rule quarantining inbound mail claiming your domain that fails DMARC
Block the spoofing source IPs at the gateway
eradication: Fix SPF includes and DKIM signing for legitimate senders flagged in aggregate reports
Move the domain DMARC policy toward p=reject once legitimate senders align
Publish null SPF and DMARC reject for parked domains
recovery: Confirm legitimate senders such as marketing and ticketing still deliver after the policy change
Track DMARC report pass rates daily for two weeks
Tell users that internal-looking mail failing checks will now be quarantined
lessons: Record why the gateway delivered DMARC-failing mail and fix the policy override
Add a detection for inbound mail with header From your domain arriving from external IPs
Set a target date for p=reject across every company domain

splunk.title: Inbound mail claiming the company domain that failed DMARC
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="*@<your_domain>" NOT All_Email.src_ip IN (<authorized_sender_ips>) by All_Email.src_ip All_Email.subject All_Email.recipient All_Email.action

splunk.title: DMARC aggregate failures by source IP
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=dmarc:aggregate header_from=<your_domain> (spf_result!=pass OR dkim_result!=pass) earliest=-14d | stats sum(count) as messages values(disposition) as disposition by source_ip | sort - messages

playbooks.name: HR or payroll themed phish asking staff to confirm pay details
playbooks.summary: Use when a lure posing as HR, benefits enrollment or payroll asked staff to sign in to view a pay slip, bonus letter or policy update, targeting employee portal credentials.

preparation: Require MFA and new-device alerts on the HR and payroll portal
Ask HR to tell the SOC before any real mass email about pay, bonuses or benefits
Log changes to bank account and tax details in the payroll system
identification: Confirm with HR that no real pay or benefits email was sent at that time
Identify whether the fake page imitates the corporate SSO or the HR portal itself
Find users who submitted credentials and check HR portal logins from new IPs
Review payroll audit logs for direct deposit changes since the lure arrived
containment: Lock direct deposit changes for affected users until each is verified
Reset credentials and sessions for users who submitted the form
Purge the lure and block its domains
eradication: Reverse any unverified bank detail change after confirming with the employee by phone
Remove attacker MFA devices from SSO and the HR portal
Have HR send a notice from a known sender confirming the earlier message was fake
recovery: Confirm the next pay run goes to the correct accounts for affected employees
Lift the change lock once each user has re-verified their details
Escalate to the payroll diversion playbook if a change was already processed
lessons: Require out-of-band confirmation for any direct deposit change made after a new-device login
Track how many staff reported versus submitted on this lure
Add a detection for HR portal logins followed by a bank change within an hour

splunk.title: HR portal logins from new IPs after the lure
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=<hr_portal> Authentication.user IN (<recipient_list>) by Authentication.user Authentication.src | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Direct deposit changes since the campaign
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<payroll_audit> action IN (bank_account_change, direct_deposit_update) earliest=-7d | table _time user employee_id src_ip old_account_last4 new_account_last4

playbooks.name: MFA push bombing after a phished password
playbooks.summary: Use when a user is flooded with MFA push requests they did not start, meaning the attacker already has the password, typically from an earlier phish, and is trying to wear them down.

preparation: Enable number matching or verified push in the MFA provider
Teach staff to deny unexpected prompts and report them with a one-click option
Alert when one user receives more than five denied pushes in ten minutes
identification: Count push requests, denials and approvals for the user and record the source IPs
Check if any push was approved and whether a session started from that IP
Find the original phish or leak where the password was exposed
Look for the same source IPs pushing to other users
containment: Reset the user's password to stop new push requests
Revoke sessions if any push was approved
Block the source IPs at the identity provider
eradication: Remove MFA factors added after an approved push
Check for mailbox rules, OAuth grants or VPN connections from the attacker session
Reset passwords for other users the same IPs targeted
recovery: Move the user to number-matching or FIDO2 before re-enabling
Thank the user if they reported and explain what happened
Monitor for renewed push attempts for 14 days
lessons: Record whether number matching was enabled for this user and why not
Measure time from first push to password reset
Add a detection for an approved push following several denials

splunk.title: Push requests and denials per user
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 eventType IN (system.push.send_factor_verify_push, user.mfa.okta_verify.deny_push, user.authentication.auth_via_mfa) actor.alternateId=<suspect_user> earliest=-24h | bin _time span=10m | stats count by _time eventType outcome.result client.ipAddress

splunk.title: Denied pushes followed by approval
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin status.errorCode=500121 earliest=-24h | stats count as denied by userPrincipalName ipAddress | join type=inner userPrincipalName [search index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin status.errorCode=0 earliest=-24h | stats latest(_time) as approved by userPrincipalName] | where denied>3

playbooks.name: HTML smuggling attachment assembled malware in the browser
playbooks.summary: Use when an HTML attachment used JavaScript to build and download a ZIP, ISO or script locally, avoiding gateway file scanning, and a user may have run the result.

preparation: Sandbox HTML attachments with JavaScript execution enabled, not just static scans
Enable EDR alerts for browser processes writing archives or disk images to Downloads
Block execution of scripts from the Downloads folder with ASR or AppLocker
identification: Run the HTML file in a sandbox and capture the file it generates
Hash the generated payload and check whether it matches any file on endpoints
Find hosts where the browser wrote the payload filename to Downloads
Trace whether the user mounted or extracted the payload and what ran next
containment: Isolate hosts where the payload ran
Add the generated payload hash and HTML attachment hash to EDR block lists
Purge the HTML attachment from all mailboxes
eradication: Remove payload files and persistence from affected hosts
Block the C2 indicators from the payload's sandbox run
Reset credentials for users logged on to affected hosts
recovery: Return cleaned hosts after a full EDR scan
Hunt for the payload filename pattern across endpoints for 30 days
Notify recipients who did not run the file that it was malicious
lessons: Record whether the gateway scanned the HTML dynamically or only statically
Add a detection for browsers writing ISO or ZIP files followed by script execution
Consider quarantining all inbound HTML attachments from external senders

splunk.title: Browser writing archives or images to Downloads
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=11 Image IN ("*chrome.exe", "*msedge.exe", "*firefox.exe") TargetFilename IN ("*\\Downloads\\*.iso", "*\\Downloads\\*.zip", "*\\Downloads\\*.img", "*\\Downloads\\*.js") | stats count by host User TargetFilename

splunk.title: Recipients of the HTML attachment
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.file_name IN ("*.htm", "*.html") All_Email.file_hash="<attachment_hash>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.action

playbooks.name: Password-protected archive attachment with the password in the email body
playbooks.summary: Use when a phish carried an encrypted ZIP or 7z with the password in the message text, so the gateway could not inspect it and the user extracted and ran the contents.

preparation: Configure the gateway to quarantine encrypted archives from external senders by default
Let the gateway try passwords found in the message body against attached archives
Log archive extraction tool launches on endpoints
identification: Extract the archive in a sandbox using the password from the email and hash each file
Find which recipients saved and extracted the archive using EDR file events
Trace the process tree after extraction on each affected host
Search for the same password string across mail to find other campaign waves
containment: Isolate hosts that executed the extracted payload
Purge all messages carrying the archive and the matching password text
Block the extracted payload hashes in EDR
eradication: Remove payload files and persistence from affected endpoints
Reset credentials cached on affected hosts
Block network indicators found during sandbox detonation
recovery: Return hosts after clean scans and confirm the user's files are intact
Release legitimate encrypted archives only after sender verification
Hunt for the payload hashes for 30 days
lessons: Decide whether encrypted archives from outside should be blocked unless the sender is allow-listed
Add a detection for archive tools extracting to temp followed by script or executable launch
Track how many legitimate business processes rely on encrypted archives

splunk.title: Inbound encrypted archives
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.file_name IN ("*.zip", "*.7z", "*.rar") All_Email.src_user="<sender>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.file_name All_Email.file_hash All_Email.action

splunk.title: Execution after archive extraction
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN (7zfm.exe, 7zg.exe, winrar.exe, explorer.exe) Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path

playbooks.name: Phishing page hosted on a trusted SaaS or form-builder platform
playbooks.summary: Use when the phishing page lives on a reputable service such as a form builder, website builder or note-sharing site, so domain reputation checks pass and blocking the whole domain is not practical.

preparation: Make sure the proxy can block by full URL path, not only by domain
Keep abuse-report contacts for common form and site-builder platforms
Decide in advance which builder platforms the business actually needs
identification: Record the exact page URL and the account or project ID on the platform
Check if the page asks for corporate passwords, MFA codes or payment details
Find users who visited that specific path and those who submitted the form
Search mail for other links to the same platform account or project ID
containment: Block the specific URL path at the proxy while leaving the platform reachable
Purge messages linking to the page
Reset credentials for users who submitted the form
eradication: Report the page to the platform's abuse team and request the account be removed
Remove attacker MFA registrations from affected accounts
Add a gateway rule that flags messages linking to form builders with login wording
recovery: Confirm the page has been taken down and remove the temporary path block later
Tell staff that real company logins never happen on form builder sites
Monitor for new pages on the same platform using the same lure text
lessons: Track which trusted platforms are most abused in your mail flow
Decide whether rarely used builder platforms should be blocked outright with exceptions
Add a detection for POST requests to form builder domains from users who just clicked an email link

splunk.title: Visits and submissions to the hosted lure
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<platform_domain>/<project_path>*" by Web.user Web.src

splunk.title: Mail linking to the platform account
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.url="*<platform_domain>/<project_path>*" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject

playbooks.name: IT administrator phished and privileged credentials exposed
playbooks.summary: Use when the phished user holds admin roles in the identity provider, cloud console or domain, so the blast radius covers the whole tenant and every minute matters.

preparation: Keep admin roles on separate cloud-only accounts that do not receive email
Require phishing-resistant MFA and privileged access workstations for admin roles
Keep two break-glass accounts that are excluded from Conditional Access and monitored
identification: List every role the phished user holds, including PIM-eligible roles
Review directory audit logs for role assignments, app registrations and policy edits since the click
Check whether Conditional Access, MFA or federation settings were changed
Look for new service principal secrets or certificates added by the user
Review on-premises domain admin activity if the account is synced
containment: Remove the user's admin role assignments immediately and revoke their sessions
Reset the password and disable the account until MFA is re-registered on a hardware key
Revert any Conditional Access or federation changes made after the click
Rotate secrets on app registrations the user could modify
eradication: Remove any accounts, role assignments or apps created by the attacker
Check for new federated domains or cross-tenant access settings
Rotate break-glass account passwords if their details could have been read
recovery: Restore admin roles only through PIM with approval and time limits
Run a full tenant configuration comparison against the last known-good export
Keep heightened alerting on directory changes for 30 days
lessons: Record why an admin account could receive and click a phish
Add a detection for any role assignment change outside the PIM workflow
Track how many admins still use the same account for mail and administration

playbooks.name: Device code phishing tricked a user into authorizing an attacker
playbooks.summary: Use when a user was sent a device login code and entered it at the genuine Microsoft device login page, which handed tokens to the attacker without exposing a password.

preparation: Block the device code flow with Conditional Access for users who do not need it
Log Entra sign-ins including the authentication protocol field
Brief staff that a request to enter a code at microsoft.com/devicelogin from a stranger is an attack
identification: Find sign-ins with authenticationProtocol deviceCode for the user and record IP and app
Compare the device code sign-in IP with the user's normal locations
List Graph, Exchange and SharePoint activity using tokens from that session
Identify how the code was delivered, such as email, Teams or a fake meeting invite
containment: Revoke the user's refresh tokens and sessions
Apply a Conditional Access block on device code flow for the affected group
Block the attacker IPs in a named location policy
eradication: Remove any device registered to Entra using the stolen token
Delete mailbox rules or app consents made during the attacker session
Search for other users with device code sign-ins from the same IPs
recovery: Confirm the user's devices list contains only known devices
Allow device code flow only for named kiosks or conference room devices
Watch for repeat device code attempts against the same user group
lessons: Record how many legitimate device code sign-ins exist so the block can be made tenant-wide
Add a detection for device code sign-ins from IPs not seen for the user before
Include device code lures in phishing awareness material

splunk.title: Devices registered after the device code sign-in

playbooks.name: Phishing kit found hosted on the company's own web server
playbooks.summary: Use when an outside party reports that a phishing page is being served from one of your domains or servers, often through a vulnerable CMS plugin or abandoned subdomain.

preparation: Keep an inventory of all public web servers, CMS instances and subdomains with owners
Send web server access logs and file integrity alerts to the SIEM
Publish a security.txt with a contact for abuse reports
identification: Confirm the reported URL is served from your infrastructure and record the file path
Copy the kit directory and its config to find where it sends harvested credentials
Review web server logs for the upload request and the vulnerability used
Check access logs for visitors who submitted data to the kit
Look for web shells or other dropped files on the same server
containment: Remove public access to the kit directory or take the site offline
Preserve a disk snapshot of the server before cleanup
Block the kit's exfiltration endpoint at the egress firewall
eradication: Patch or remove the vulnerable CMS plugin used to upload the kit
Delete the kit and any web shells, and rotate CMS admin and hosting credentials
Rebuild the server from a known-good image if a web shell was found
recovery: Request delisting from safe-browsing and spam block lists once the kit is gone
Tell the reporting party and any listed takedown services that the page is removed
Monitor the server's file integrity alerts for 30 days
lessons: Record how long the kit was live before the first report
Add a detection for new PHP or HTML files written under the web root outside deployments
Decommission abandoned sites and dangling subdomains found during the review
